Surah 19, verses 1–4:

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾. We have already discussed the disjointed letters (huruf al-hijaʾ) at the beginning of al-Baqarah. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib used to say in his supplication: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-ʿAyn-Sad." So it is possible that this sequence, in his view, is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, or that he was calling upon the names from which these letters were taken.

﴿Dhikr﴾ (a mention). Its implied sense is: "This is a mention of ﴿His servant Zakariya﴾." He described him with servanthood as an honour for him, and as a notice of his being singled out and brought near. "His servant" is in the accusative as the object of "raḥmah" (mercy), since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has been annexed to its agent and so governs its object in the accusative. It has also been said that it is the object of a hidden verb, meaning "the mercy of His servant," and on this view one stops at what precedes it. This view is weak, since it involves the unnecessary assumption of a hidden verb and detaching the governing word from its governance after it has been prepared to govern.

﴿When he called out to his Lord﴾, meaning he called upon Him, ﴿with a hidden call﴾, concealing it, because He hears the hidden just as He hears the audible, and because concealment is closer to sincerity and further from ostentation, and so that people would not blame him for seeking a child.

﴿The bone has weakened﴾, meaning it became feeble. ﴿And the head has flared up with white hair﴾: a metaphor for grey hair drawn from the blazing of fire. ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾, meaning: I have been fortunate in my prayers to You previously, so answer me in this matter as well. Thus he sought means to Allah through His earlier kindness to him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 16–21:

﴿And mention in the Book Maryam﴾ This is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), and "the Book" means the Qur'an. ﴿When she withdrew from her family﴾ meaning she isolated herself from them and secluded herself away from them. ﴿To an eastern place﴾ meaning toward the direction of the east. ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ meaning Jibril (Gabriel). It was said: it means ʿIsa (Jesus). The first view is the correct one, because Jibril is the one who appeared to her in human form, by consensus. ﴿She said: "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are one who fears Allah."﴾ When she saw the angel who had appeared to her in the form of a man, having entered upon her, she feared that he might be one of the children of Adam, so she said this statement to him. Its meaning: if you are one who fears Allah, then keep away from me, for I seek refuge in Allah from you. It was also said: "if you are one who fears Allah" refers to a man known among them for wickedness, but this view is weak and far-fetched. ﴿To give you a pure boy.﴾ The pure boy is ʿIsa, peace be upon him. It is recited as "liyahaba" with the yaʾ, in which case the subject is the pronoun for the Lord, glorified and exalted be He. It is also recited with the first-person hamza ("li-ahaba"), in which case the speaker is Jibril. He attributed the giving to himself because he is the one whom Allah sent with it, or he may have said that as a report on behalf of Allah, exalted be He. ﴿And I have not been a fornicating woman﴾ Al-baghiyy is the woman who openly commits adultery, and the form of baghiyy is fa'ul (fa'ūl). ﴿And that We may make him a sign﴾ The pronoun refers to the child, and the lam is connected to an implied element, its estimated sense being: "We do that so that We may make him a sign."

﴿فَحَمَلَتْهُ﴾ means: in her womb. The period of her pregnancy was eight months. Ibn 'Abbas said: she carried him and gave birth to him within an hour. ﴿مَكَاناً قَصِيّاً﴾ means a distant place. She withdrew far away out of modesty before her people, lest they think ill of her. ﴿فَأَجَآءَهَا﴾ means: she was driven or compelled to it. It is derived from *jā'a* with the causative *hamzah* (*hamzat al-ta'diyah*, the hamza that makes a verb transitive). ﴿ٱلْمَخَاضُ﴾ means the labour pains, that is, childbirth (*al-nifas*). ﴿إِلَىٰ جِذْعِ ٱلنَّخْلَةِ﴾ It is reported that she embraced the trunk of the palm tree because of the severity of her labour pains. ﴿قَالَتْ يٰلَيْتَنِي مِتُّ﴾ She only wished for death out of fear of her people's denial and their suspicion of her, and of their falling upon her blood. ﴿وَكُنتُ نَسْياً﴾ *Nisy* means a worthless thing that is not regarded. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it in this way. It is also said that it refers to 'Isa, since *sarī* means a noble man. ﴿وَهُزِّىۤ إِلَيْكِ بِجِذْعِ ٱلنَّخْلَةِ﴾ The trunk was dry, but God created fresh dates on it as an honour to her and as a comfort. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verse 41–47:

﴿Ṣiddīqan﴾ is an intensive form (binā' mubālagha) derived from truthfulness (al-ṣidq) or from affirmation (al-taṣdīq). He is described as ṣiddīq before revelation, and he was made a prophet (nubbi'a) after it. It is also possible that he combined both attributes. ﴿That which neither hears nor sees﴾ refers to the idols. ﴿A straight path﴾ means an upright, right course. ﴿I will surely stone you﴾: it is said that this means stoning with rocks, and it is said that it means reviling. ﴿And leave me for a long time﴾ means for a lengthy period. The phrase "and leave me" is conjoined with an omitted clause, whose implied meaning is: "beware of my stoning you." ﴿He said: Peace be upon you﴾: this is a farewell of parting. It is also said that it means a pact of peace, not a greeting, because it is not permissible for a disbeliever to be greeted with salam first. ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you﴾: this is a promise, and it is what is alluded to in His saying, "out of a promise he had made to him" (Q. 9:114). Ibn 'Atiyya said its meaning is: "I will supplicate Allah to guide you, and He will forgive you for your faith," because seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is not permissible. It is also said that he promised to seek forgiveness for him despite his disbelief, and perhaps he had not known that Allah does not forgive the disbelievers until He informed him of that. This view is strengthened by His saying: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾ (Q. 26:86). A similar statement is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Abu Talib: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you." ﴿Ḥafiyyan﴾ means kind and gentle to him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 61–62:

﴿Bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen): i.e., he informed them of those things that were hidden from them. ﴿Ma'tiyyan﴾ (that which will be reached): its form is that of the passive participle (maf'ul). It has been said that it carries the sense of the active participle (fa'il), because it is the promise that comes (ya'ti). It has also been said that it retains its own sense, because the promise is Paradise, and they come to it.

﴿Laghwan﴾ (idle talk): i.e., worthless speech. ﴿Illa salaman﴾ (except the word "peace"): an exceptional (munqati') istithna', meaning the exception is not of the same kind as what precedes it.

It has also been said that the meaning is that provision comes to them at every time they need it, and this is expressed by "morning and evening" in accordance with people's customary times for eating.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verse 64:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ This is the report of the words of Jibril (Gabriel) when he was absent from the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to him: "You were slow to come to me, and I longed for you." He said: "I was more longing, but I am a servant who is commanded: when I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I seek reward (from God)."

And this verse was revealed: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us, and what is behind us, and what is between that﴾. That is, to Him belongs what is in front of us, what is behind us, and what we are in of directions and places; so we have no moving from one place to another except by the command of God. It is also said: "what is before us" is the world until the first blast in the Trumpet (al-Sur); "what is behind us" is the Hereafter; and "what is between that" is what lies between the two blasts. It is also said: "what is before us" refers to our past deeds and "what remains of them," and the state we are in. The first interpretation is more fitting to the context of the verse.

﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾: it is on the pattern of fa'il (fa'il) from forgetting (al-nisyan), in the sense of heedlessness (al-dhuhul). It is also said it means abandoning (al-tark), and the first is more evident.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 65–66:

﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ That is, any equal or counterpart. It is taken from al-musami and al-mudahi (one who is comparable or equal). It has also been said: [it means] one who is called by His name, because no one has been given the name of Allah except Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ This is a report of the saying of one who denies resurrection from the graves. "Man" here is a generic term, intended to refer to the disbelievers. It has also been said that the one who said this was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it has been said [it was] Umayya ibn Khalaf. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 65–66:

﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ That is, any equal or counterpart. It is taken from al-musami and al-mudahi (one who is comparable or equal). It has also been said: [it means] one who is called by His name, because no one has been given the name of Allah except Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ This is a report of the saying of one who denies resurrection from the graves. "Man" here is a generic term, intended to refer to the disbelievers. It has also been said that the one who said this was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it has been said [it was] Umayya ibn Khalaf. The hamza that entered upon the phrase ﴿a-idha ma mittu﴾ ("when I have died") is for denial and disbelief. The lam in His words ﴿la-sawfa ukhraj﴾ ("shall I really be brought forth") was brought in as a report of the statement of those who held this meaning, and "bringing forth" (al-ikhraj) is intended to mean resurrection (al-ba'th).

Does man not remember that We created him before? This is an argument for the truth of resurrection and a refutation of those who deny it, because the first creation is evidence for the second. ﴿And surely We will gather them, and the devils too﴾, meaning their companion devils who misled them. The *wa* (and) is either conjunctive, or it means "together with," in which case *al-shayatin* (the devils) is a *maf'ul ma'ahu* (object of accompaniment). ﴿On their knees﴾: *jithiyyan* is the plural of *jath*, and its pattern is *maf'ul*, from your saying *jatha al-rajul* when the man sits the sitting of one who is humbled and afraid. ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every group﴾. *Al-shi'a* (group) is a company of people who agree on a creed or on following a person. The meaning of the verse is that God drags out from every group its most rebellious member and sends him forward to the Fire. Some scholars said: the meaning is that We begin with the one greatest in crime, then the one greatest in crime after him. ﴿Which of them﴾: its *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) has been disputed. Sibawayh said it is *mabni 'ala al-damm* (indeclinable, built on the *damma*), because the pronoun referring back to it from the relative clause has been omitted, and the implied sense is "which of them is more severe," so it was required to be indeclinable. Al-Khalil said it is *marfu'* (in the nominative) by way of *hikaya* (quotation), its estimated sense being "the one about whom it is said, he is more severe." Yunus said the verb was suspended from it and it took the nominative as a subject. ﴿Most deserving of burning therein﴾: *al-sili* is a verbal noun from *salla al-nar* (to burn in the Fire). The meaning of the verse is that God knows who is most deserving to be burned in punishment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 71–73:

﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it (wurud)﴾. This is addressed to all people according to the majority of scholars. As for the believers, they will enter it, but it will be extinguished and will not harm them. So "wurud" in this sense means "entering," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship other than Allah will be the fuel of Hell; you will be entering it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], and ﴿and He will lead them into the Fire﴾ [Hud: 98]. It has also been said that "wurud" means "coming upon it," like His saying: ﴿and when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and the intended meaning is crossing over the Sirat (the bridge over Hell). It has also been said that the address is to the disbelievers, in which case there is no difficulty.

﴿A decree (hatman)﴾, that is, a matter that must occur. ﴿Then We will save those who were mindful of Allah (alladhina ittaqaw)﴾. If "wurud" means entering, then the salvation of those who were mindful lies in the Fire being cool and safe for them, and then in their coming out of it. If "wurud" means passing over the Sirat, then their salvation lies in their crossing safely and being spared from falling into it.

﴿Then which of the two groups is better in position (maqaman) and finer in assembly (nadiyyan)?﴾ The two groups are the believers and the disbelievers. "Maqam" is a noun of place from qama (to stand), and it has been read with a dammah as "muqam" from aqama (to dwell). "Nadi" means gathering or assembly. The meaning of the verse is that the disbelievers said to the believers: "We are better than you in position," that is, in a better state in this world, and finer in gathering; so we are more honored by Allah than you.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verse 74:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them, [generations] that were better in wealth and in outward appearance.﴾ "Kam" (how many) is the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed). The meaning of the verse is a refutation of the disbelievers in their aforementioned statement: that is, good circumstances in this world are not evidence of honour with Allah, because Allah has destroyed those who were in better circumstances than you in this world. ﴿Hum ahsanu﴾ (they were better). Al-Zamakhshari said: this clause is in the place of a accusative qualifier of "kum" (them). ﴿Athathan﴾ (furnishings), that is, household goods. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a general noun, covering property in the form of cash, goods, and livestock; it is a collective noun. It was also said that it is a plural, whose singular is "athatah." ﴿Wiyyan﴾ (outward appearance), with a silent hamza before the ya: its meaning is a fine sight, and it derives from "ru'yah" (seeing), while "ri'y" is the name of what is seen. It is also read with a doubled ya without hamza, which is a lightening of the hamza, so the meaning is the same. It was said that it derives from "rayy al-sharib" (quenching one's thirst), that is, enjoyment of drinks and food. Ibn 'Abbas read it as "ziyyan" with a zay.

﴿Let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾: that is, He gives him respite and lets him be. Scholars differ over whether this verb is a supplication (*du'a'*) or an informative statement (*khabar*) that is phrased as a command for emphasis. ﴿Until﴾ here marks the limit of the extension in misguidance. ﴿Either the punishment﴾ means the punishment of this world, ﴿[and] they will know who is worse in position and weaker in soldiers﴾, in contrast to their saying, ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 76–80:

﴿وَٱلْبَٰقِيَاتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَاتُ﴾ [And the enduring good deeds]: it is mentioned in al-Kahf [47]. ﴿وَخَيْرٌ مَّرَدّاً﴾ [and better in return]: that is, better in outcome and final result. ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتَ ٱلَّذِي كَفَرَ﴾ [Have you seen the one who disbelieved]: he is al-As ibn Wa'il. ﴿وَقَالَ لأُوتَيَنَّ مَالاً وَوَلَداً﴾ [and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"]: he had said, "If I am resurrected, as Muhammad claims, I will surely have wealth and children there." ﴿أَطَّلَعَ ٱلْغَيْبَ﴾ [Has he looked into the unseen?]: the hamza (الهمزة) is for denial and rejection of the disbeliever's claim. ﴿كَلاَّ﴾ [No!]: a rebuke against his statement. ﴿سَنَكْتُبُ مَا يَقُولُ﴾ [We will record what he says]: He put it in the future tense because the reward and punishment will only become manifest in the future. ﴿وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ ٱلْعَذَابِ مَدّاً﴾ [and We will extend for him of the punishment an extension]: that is, We will increase it for him. ﴿وَنَرِثُهُ مَا يَقُولُ﴾ [and We will inherit from him what he says]: that is, We will inherit the things he claimed he would be given in the Hereafter, namely wealth and children. Their inheritance means that the disbeliever perishes and leaves them behind. His two sons, Hisham and Amr, embraced Islam, may Allah be pleased with them both. ﴿وَيَأْتِينَا فَرْداً﴾ [and he will come to Us alone]: that is, without wealth, without children, without any protector, and without any helper.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 82–84:

﴿They will deny their worship﴾. It has been said: the pronoun in "yakfurun" (they will deny) refers to the disbelievers, and the pronoun in "ibadatihim" (their worship) refers to the deities worshipped. So the meaning is like their saying: "By Allah, we were not polytheists." It has also been said: the pronoun in "yakfurun" refers to the deities worshipped, and the pronoun in "ibadatihim" refers to the disbelievers. So the meaning is like His saying: ﴿You did not worship us﴾ [Yunus: 28].

"Wafdan" (٩٥ ﴿وَفْداً﴾): it is said that it means riding (rukbanan). The literal meaning of "wafd" is those who come (to a place), and their custom is to ride, which is why this was said. It is also said that it means honoured (mukramun), because the custom is to honour delegations.

﴿وِرْداً﴾ means thirsty (ʿiṭashan), because one who comes to water comes to it only out of thirst.

﴿لاَّ يَمْلِكُونَ ٱلشَّفَٰعَةَ﴾ The pronoun may refer to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: they do not have the ability to intercede for them. In that case "man ittakhadha" (مَنِ ٱتَّخَذَ) is an exceptive clause that is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'), meaning "but" (lakin). Or the pronoun may refer to the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), and then the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil), and the meaning is: they do not have the ability to intercede except for one who has taken a covenant, or: none of them has the ability to intercede except one who has taken a covenant. Or the pronoun may refer to both groups, since both have been mentioned before; then the exception is also connected. "Man ittakhadha" may refer to either the intercessor or the one for whom intercession is made.

"ʿAhdan" (عَهْداً): he means by it faith and righteous deeds. It may also mean permission to intercede, and this is more likely (arjah), because of His saying: ﴿no intercession will benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. Apparently this is a reference to the intercession of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Standing Place (al-mawqif), when he will stand alone in it, and other prophets will say: "Myself, myself!"

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 89–92:

﴿A dreadful thing﴾ i.e., a grievous thing. ﴿Whereby the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ i.e., they are split asunder by the saying of the disbelievers: "Allah has taken a son." ﴿And the earth is split open﴾ i.e., it collapses in ruin. ﴿Because they ascribed to the Most Merciful a son﴾ i.e., because they called upon for the Most Merciful a son. It is also recited as wuldan (وُلْدا), with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam, and this is a dialectal form.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 19, verses 93–98:

﴿Indeed, all who are in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a rebuttal of the claim of the disbelievers. The meaning is that all of them are His servants, so how could any of them be a son to Him? Here "in" (inna) is negative, and "all" (kull) is the subject, with its predicate being: ﴿come to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾.

﴿The Most Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)﴾: it is the love and acceptance that Allah places in hearts for whomever He wills of His servants. It was also said that this verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿We have made it easy in your tongue﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and "in your tongue" means in your language (lughah).

﴿That you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people contentious (ludd)﴾: "ludd" is the plural of "aladd" (lad), meaning one who is extremely quarrelsome and argumentative. What is meant by this is the Quraysh. It was also said that its meaning is "wicked" (fujjār).

﴿Do you perceive from them anyone or hear from them a faint sound (rikz)?﴾: "rikz" is a faint, hidden sound. The meaning is that no trace of them remains, and in this there is a warning to the Quraysh.
